blocks.prompt: The Rock That Knows Which Way Is North
blocks.text: A magnet has two ends. We call them poles. One is the north pole. One is the south pole. Hold two magnets together the right way and they snap shut. Turn one around and they push apart. They will not touch, no matter how hard you press. A magnet pulls on iron. It does not pull on wood or plastic or glass. Long ago, people found rocks that could pull iron all by themselves. They called them lodestones. A lodestone hung on a string will slowly turn until it points north. That is how sailors found their way home.

the two magnets push apart
it points north

blocks.prompt: The Half That Is Never Half
blocks.text: Every magnet has two poles, a north and a south. Put a north pole next to a south pole and the two magnets rush together. Put two north poles together and they shove each other away. You can feel the push in your hands even though there is nothing between them. Here is a strange part. Cut a magnet in half and you do not get one north piece and one south piece. You get two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south. Cut those in half and it happens again. Nobody has ever found a magnet with only one pole. More than a thousand years ago, people in China noticed that a certain dark rock always turned to face the same direction. They called it a lodestone. If you float a magnetized needle on a scrap of wood, it swings around and settles pointing north. That simple trick became the compass, and the compass let sailors cross open water for weeks without ever seeing land.

answers: they push each other away
two smaller magnets, each with a north and a south pole
it always turned to face the same direction

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Every iron atom acts like a tiny magnet
Heat scrambles a magnet and wipes it out
Iron loses its magnetism above 1,418 degrees Fahrenheit
Earth's core is liquid iron in motion
A compass needle lines up with Earth's field
The northern lights are that field at work

blocks.prompt: The Nail That Forgets
blocks.text: Iron is full of tiny magnets you cannot see. Every atom in it behaves like a minute bar magnet, with its own north and south. In a plain iron nail, these tiny magnets point in every direction at once. They cancel each other out, so the nail is not magnetic. Now stroke that nail with a strong magnet, always in the same direction. The tiny magnets inside start to line up. Once enough of them face the same way, their pulls add together instead of canceling, and the nail becomes a magnet. It will pick up paper clips. Drop it hard on the floor a few times, or hold it in a fire, and the tiny magnets get jostled out of line again. The nail forgets. Earth pulls the same trick on a giant scale. Deep beneath the crust, the outer core is an ocean of liquid iron, hot enough to glow but under such crushing pressure that it churns instead of boiling away. That moving metal generates a magnetic field that reaches far out into space. A compass needle simply lines up with it. The field does more than steer ships. The Sun throws out a constant stream of charged particles, and Earth's magnetic field deflects most of them around the planet. The few that slip through near the poles crash into the air high above and make it glow, which is what the northern lights are.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Oersted, 1820: an electric current makes magnetism
Faraday, 1831: a moving magnet makes electricity
Nearly all electricity is made by spinning magnets
A motor is a generator run backward
Neodymium magnets, invented in 1982, are the strongest

blocks.prompt: The Twitch That Built the Modern World
blocks.text: For most of history, magnetism was a curiosity. A lodestone could drag a nail across a table and point a ship toward home, and that was about the end of it. Nobody suspected it had anything to do with electricity. That changed in 1820, during a lecture. A Danish professor named Hans Christian Oersted was demonstrating an electric current when he noticed that a compass needle sitting nearby twitched every time he switched the current on. It swung sideways, not toward the wire. Oersted had stumbled onto something enormous: an electric current makes a magnetic field, and the field wraps around the wire in circles. Electricity and magnetism were not two separate mysteries. They were one. Eleven years later, Michael Faraday ran the discovery backward. If a current could make magnetism, could magnetism make a current? He wound wire into a coil and pushed a bar magnet through it. The needle on his meter jumped, but only while the magnet was moving. Hold it still and the current died. Motion was the missing ingredient. That is a small result with a very long shadow. Almost all the electricity in your house was made by Faraday's trick. A power plant does not create energy out of nothing. It boils water, or catches wind, or drops river water through a turbine, and every bit of that effort goes into one job: spinning magnets past coils of wire. Coal, gas, nuclear fuel, and wind turbines differ only in how they turn the shaft. Run the same machine in reverse and you have an electric motor. Feed current into coils near magnets and the push between them turns the shaft instead. The fan, the drill, the blender, the electric car, the hard drive that stored your photos, the speaker vibrating in your headphones right now: all magnets, all doing the same fundamental thing. Look closer and the two ideas collapse into one. A magnetic field is simply what moving electric charge looks like, and inside iron the charge that moves is the electrons themselves, spinning in place. Every magnet on your refrigerator is, in a sense, a very small and very patient electric current that has been running since the atom formed.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Rock That Knows Which Way Is North

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Earth's outer core: liquid iron, about 1,800 miles down
Gilbert's terrella, 1600: the Earth itself is a magnet
The field has flipped hundreds of times
Last full reversal: about 780,000 years ago
Seafloor magnetic stripes proved continents move
Mars lost its dynamo, then lost its air

blocks.prompt: The Field We Live Inside
blocks.text: Hold a compass and you are running an experiment on the entire planet. The needle is a small magnet, free to swing, and it settles along a field generated roughly 1,800 miles beneath your shoes. Nothing about that is obvious, and for most of human history nobody understood it. Sailors used the compass for four hundred years before anyone could say what it was pointing at. The first serious answer came from William Gilbert, physician to Queen Elizabeth I. In 1600 he carved a sphere out of lodestone, called it a terrella, or little Earth, and walked a small compass across its surface. The needle behaved exactly as ships' compasses behaved on the ocean, dipping steeply near the poles and lying flat near the equator. Gilbert drew the obvious conclusion and published it: the Earth itself is a magnet. He was right, and his reasoning was sound, but his mechanism was wrong. He assumed the core was a colossal lodestone. It cannot be. Iron loses its magnetism above about 1,418 degrees Fahrenheit, and Earth's core is several times hotter than that. A permanent magnet could not survive down there for a single day. The field must therefore be generated continuously, and it is. The outer core is an ocean of liquid iron and nickel roughly 1,400 miles thick, stirred by heat rising from below and twisted by the planet's rotation. Moving metal carries electric current, current makes magnetism, and that magnetism helps steer the very flow that produces it. The whole arrangement feeds on itself. Geologists call it the geodynamo, and it has been running, with interruptions, for billions of years. Those interruptions are the strangest part of the story. Every few hundred thousand years, on no fixed schedule, the field weakens, wanders, and flips. North becomes south. We know this because lava remembers. When molten rock cools and hardens, the magnetic minerals inside it freeze into alignment with whatever field is present at that moment, locking in a record that outlasts everyone who might have doubted it. In the 1960s, ships towing magnetometers across the Atlantic found that the seafloor was striped: bands of rock magnetized north, then south, then north again, running parallel to the mid-ocean ridge and mirrored on both sides of it. New crust was welling up at the ridge, taking a snapshot of the field as it cooled, and spreading outward in two directions like a pair of tape recorders. Those stripes did not merely confirm that the field reverses. They proved that continents move, an idea still unfashionable at the time. The field is not steady even now. Magnetic north has drifted out of Arctic Canada and is heading for Siberia at speeds that have reached 30 miles per year, fast enough that navigation systems must be corrected on a schedule. The last full reversal was about 780,000 years ago, which makes the current calm interval long by historical standards. None of this would matter much if the field were only a navigation aid. It is also a shield. The Sun blows a thin, fast wind of charged particles across the solar system, and Earth's field turns most of it aside, forming a teardrop-shaped bubble called the magnetosphere that streams out for hundreds of thousands of miles on the night side. Particles that leak in near the poles collide with the upper atmosphere and make it glow, which is the aurora. Mars, whose dynamo shut down billions of years ago, has no such bubble, and the solar wind has been stripping its air away ever since. The difference between a living planet and a dry one may come down to whether the iron in its heart is still moving.
